extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, designers, and critics interested in aesthetic principles of architectural ornament and color
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive aesthetic guidance for architectural form, ornamentation, and the use of color: when and how to abstract imitated forms, how much finish to allow, how to place color, and a checklist of characteristics composing Power and Beauty in buildings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful proportions are unique
rubrics_metrics.description: All beautiful proportions are unique, they are not general formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on fixed formulas for proportion; treat proportion as a unique solution for each building rather than a repeatable general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction of imitated form (degree determined by place and circumstance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstraction of imitated form is partly involuntary in early art and becomes a matter of free will later; how far imitation is carried towards completeness depends upon place and various circumstances rather than on general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide abstraction level according to the object's intended place, viewing distance, and role in the composition. Use only so much of an imitated detail as is 'good for his architecture,' allowing no more. Examples: highly abstract leafage on mouldings intended for distance; more complete ivy leaves where seen closer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether architecture frames sculpture or sculpture ornaments architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is first to be clearly determined whether the architecture is a frame for the sculpture, or the sculpture an ornament of the architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sculpture is an ornament of architecture, it should not aim to represent its subject fully but to gather arrangements of form pleasing to the eye in their intended places. Let subordination of sculpture to architecture guide its treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry is not abstraction; do not confuse regularity with architectural abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetry is not abstraction. Leaves may be carved in the most regular order and yet be meanly imitative; or thrown wild and loose and yet be highly architectural in separate treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ornament by whether only necessary character is given for suggestion and architectural lines are achieved, not by mere symmetry. Use flow and outline to judge nobility rather than symmetry alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of finish should correspond to viewing distance and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearness to the eye influences architectural abstraction: mouldings or figures meant to be seen from a distance may be more abstract, while parts placed close to the eye may be carried to utmost completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place more detailed, finished sculpture where viewers will see it closely; leave distant elements more abstract. Example: lateral buttress moulding designed for 40–50 feet is more abstract than ornaments near the gate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest imitation should be of the noblest objects only
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest imitation shall be of the noblest object. It is good judgment to proportion completeness of execution of parts to the formality of the whole, and to imitate only natural forms, and those the noblest, in the completed parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid faithful imitation of ugly or unnatural subjects; reserve high finish for noble natural forms (animals, flowers) and avoid making trivial or ugly objects the focus of refined imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion execution of parts to the formality of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Since five or six leaves must stand for a tree, let also five or six touches stand for a leaf: proportion the completeness of execution of parts to the formality of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplify parts proportionally to the abstraction of the whole: if the whole is formal or reduced, make each part correspondingly simplified in touch and detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial subjects (gargoyles, bosses) should be treated abstractly; whole small animals can be fully finished
rubrics_metrics.description: If an animal form be in a gargoyle or a head only for a boss, its sculpture will be highly abstract; but if it be an entire animal, small and near the eye, its sculpture may rightly be carried to the utmost possible completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide finish by completeness and visibility of the subject: detached, whole, and near subjects merit more complete modeling; partial or emerging forms should remain more abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting ornament dominate composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment the architect allows himself to dwell on the imitated portions, there is a chance of his losing sight of the duty of his ornament ... His architecture has become a mere framework for the setting of delicate sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitative ornament as the extreme of grace in language: do not obtain ornament at the cost of purpose, meaning, force, or conciseness. Ensure ornament serves composition and does not become cabinet sculpture transplanted to a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design process: begin in severe abstraction and mark parts for high finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Design all things at first in severe abstraction, and be prepared, if need were, to carry them out in that form; then mark the parts where high finish would be admissible, complete these always with stern reference to their general effect, and connect them by a graduated scale of abstraction with the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hierarchical workflow: abstract overall design first, identify focal elements for careful finish, and ensure transitions between degrees of finish are graduated and compositionally driven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never imitate anything but natural forms in completed parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Never imitate anything but natural forms, and those the noblest, in the completed parts. The degradation of renaissance decoration arose from imitation of ugly, i.e. unnatural things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict high-finish imitation to noble natural forms (flowers, animals). Avoid armor, musical instruments, meaningless scrolls, and other fanciful/unrelated objects as principal subjects for refined sculptural finishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture is imperfect without color; prefer natural stone colors
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot consider architecture as in any wise perfect without color. The colors of architecture should be those of natural stones; partly because more durable, but also because more perfect and graceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor natural colored stones for façades and patterning over mechanically applied paint; avoid relying on painted color unless exceptional painterly skill is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on decorative painting by common workmen
rubrics_metrics.description: The laying of color by a mechanical hand, and its toning under a vulgar eye, are far more offensive than rudeness in cutting the stone. The latter is imperfection only; the former deadness or discordance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If painting cannot be executed by a master painter, sacrifice some intricacy of design to employ nobler material (natural stone) rather than risk crude painted ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the building as a single organism for color
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider our building as a kind of organized creature; in coloring which we must look to the single and separately organized creatures of Nature, not to her landscape combinations. Our building, if it is well composed, is one thing, and is to be colored as Nature would color one thing--a shell, a flower, or an animal; not as she colors groups of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose an overall color scheme treating the entire building as a single entity rather than a patchwork of unrelated colored parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of color from form
rubrics_metrics.description: The first great principle of architectural color: Let it be visibly independent of form. Never paint a column with vertical lines, but always cross it. Never give separate mouldings separate colors ... but vary both the ground and the figures with the same harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design color patterns on principles distinct from the moulding or architectural lines: colors should form an independent 'system' that occasionally coincides with form but chiefly runs its own course. Avoid coloring that merely follows or emphasizes architectural contours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place color on broad surfaces and simplify where form is rich
rubrics_metrics.description: The best place for color is on broad surfaces, not on the points of interest in form. In all cases it is a safe rule to simplify color when form is rich, and vice versa; and I think it would be well in general to carve all capitals and graceful ornaments in white marble, and so leave them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve complex carving for white marble or uncolored finishes; deploy variegated color boldly on flat walls and shafts, but keep capitals and mouldings simpler in color to avoid visual conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color must be arranged in simple masses, zones, cloudings, or spots
rubrics_metrics.description: If architectural color is to be beautiful as its form was, we are limited to simple masses of it, to zones, as in the rainbow and the zebra; cloudings and flamings, as in marble shells and plumage, or spots of various shapes and dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting refined linear color patterns that mimic refined form; prefer broad, simple color shapes (zones, chequers, spots, flaming patterns) whose effectiveness depends on quantity and juxtaposition rather than delicate outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color outlines should be soft or simple; refined outlines deaden color
rubrics_metrics.description: Color, to be perfect, must have a soft outline or a simple one: it cannot have a refined one; you will never produce a good painted window with good figure-drawing in it. You will lose perfection of color as you give perfection of line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing painted or colored elements, avoid refined, delicate outlines for color areas. Prefer simpler, often angular or geometric boundaries that let color sing without competing with precise line-drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curved outlines and refined form deaden and confuse color; angular patterns are often better
rubrics_metrics.description: Curved outlines, especially if refined, deaden the color, and confuse the mind. Triangular and barred forms are therefore convenient, or others the simplest possible; leaving the pleasure of the spectator to be taken in the color, and in that only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For color-patterned surfaces choose angular, geometric, or simple motifs rather than refined curves; many forms reproved in sculpture are excellent as color patterns (e.g., Tudor reticulation in color).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monochrome design as intermediate between coloring and carving
rubrics_metrics.description: Monochrome design is the intermediate condition between coloring and carving, admitting for the first time the color to be concurrent with its outlines; that is to say ... the entire figure to be detached in one color from a ground of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use monochrome (inlaid or single-color relief) where outline-only figures are desired; but recognize its limits and place it appropriately among other decorative modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold scale of architectural decoration (organic-form → color-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations of the entire system of architectural decoration: 1. Organic form dominant: true, independent sculpture and alto-relievo; elaborate in completion of form, not abstract, and either to be left in pure white marble, or most cautiously touched with color in points and borders only, in a system not concurrent with their forms. 2. Organic form sub-dominant: basso-relievo or intaglio; more abstract in proportion to reduction of depth; touched with color more boldly, still non-concurrent with forms. 3. Organic form abstracted to outline: monochrome design; entire figure detached in one color from a ground of another. 4. Organic forms entirely lost: geometrical patterns or variable cloudings in the most vivid color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place decorative modes along this scale according to depth, completeness, and intended effect. Use white marble sculpture for highest form; reserve vivid color for surfaces where organic form is lost and geometric pattern is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial subject becomes principal and must be left to the painter
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial subject, without such abstraction, becomes necessarily principal, or, at all events, ceases to be the architect's concern; its plan must be left to the painter after the completion of the building, as in the works of Veronese and Giorgione on the palaces of Venice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pictorial painting cannot be given an appropriately abstract, architectural mode (e.g., mosaic), accept that it will dominate and be the painter's responsibility; do not try to make fully pictorial painting serve purely architectural ends unless the pictorial mode is intentionally archaic/abstract (e.g., Byzantine mosaics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monochrome and excessive abstraction are progressive or imperfect arts; prefer high sculpture plus pattern color
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive degree of abstraction in monochrome figures necessitates placing them as a progressive or imperfect art, and a perfect building should rather be composed of the highest sculpture (organic form dominant and sub-dominant), associated with pattern colors on the flat or broad surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor the combination of finished sculpture and geometrical/patterned color fields over reliance on monochrome abstraction for architectural dignity and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture and color should set off each other by opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The grace of the carved forms is best seen when it is thus boldly opposed to severe traceries of color, while the color itself is, as we have seen, always most piquant when it is put into sharp angular arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose relationships so sculpture (white marble, refined form) contrasts with angular, vivid color patterns on adjoining surfaces to enhance both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture's nobility depends on visible expression of intellectual life
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects become noble or ignoble in proportion to the fulness of the life which either they themselves enjoy, or of whose action they bear the evidence. Architecture ... depend[s], for their dignity and pleasurableness in the utmost degree, upon the vivid expression of the intellectual life which has been concerned in their production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for visible signs of honest, vigorous intellectual labor and design in the work; buildings should manifest the mind and judgment of their maker rather than appear mechanistic or merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true life from false/feigned life in works
rubrics_metrics.description: When we begin to be concerned with the energies of man, we find ourselves dealing with a double creature ... He has a true and false (otherwise called a living and dead, or a feigned or unfeigned) life. His true life ... is a force of assimilation which converts everything around him into food, or into instruments ... His false life ... acts, even when it cannot be said to animate, and is not always easily known from the true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to ensure that the apparent vitality of design and ornament is a genuine expression of intellect and purpose, not mere affectation or feigned 'life' that masks vacuity. Seek authenticity of creative energy in architectural work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist of noble architectural characters (Power and Beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recapitulation of conditions incidentally determined as grounds of deep impression: Considerable size, exhibited by simple terminal lines; Projection towards the top; Breadth of flat surface; Square compartments of that surface; Varied and visible masonry; Vigorous depth of shadow (especially by pierced traceries); Varied proportion in ascent; Lateral symmetry; Sculpture most delicate at the base; Enriched quantity of ornament at the top; Sculpture abstract in inferior ornaments and mouldings, complete in animal forms; Both (kinds of sculpture) to be executed in white marble; Vivid color introduced in flat geometrical patterns and obtained by the use of naturally colored stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this enumerated checklist as a compositional inventory to judge or design a building aiming at the unison of Power and Beauty. Each character should be considered for inclusion and balanced with others; examples and textual cross-references are provided in the chapter (see cited sections).
